newsitem.title: UK: British Gas readies big users for supply breaks.
newsitem.headline: British Gas readies big users for supply breaks.

text.p: British Gas' supply arm Transco has warned large industrial gas consumers that it may test their readiness for supply interruptions this winter, a major gas buyer said on Tuesday.
"Transco is thinking of having test interruptions in the early autumn to check communication channels are right and everyone responds," said the buyer.
Around 40 percent of gas supplied to industrial users in the market over 25,000 therms a year is under interruptible contracts, said Chris Partridge of U.K. energy consultants John Hall Associates.
Most long term gas contracts in the power generation sector are interruptible, he said.
Interruptible contracts are one tool used by suppliers to deal with peak winter demand.
Buyers are offered discounted transportation rates to account for the threat of supply disruption.
But during cold snaps last winter, the system ran into problems, Chris Train, energy balancing manager at Transco told Reuters.
"We had problems last winter with some (interruptible buyers) not interrupting their supplies when asked," said Train. "This puts the supply security of the whole system in jeopardy."
This winter Transco wants to ensure that all interruptible customers are genuinely prepared to switch to other fuels or cut back production if necessary.
"We're going through an exercise to see if interruptibles are true interruptibles. If we're in doubt then we will carry out a physical interuption -- as the Network Code allows us to do," said Train.
Consumers receive five hours warning of an interruption.
Buyers said they objected to being tested.
"We are quite appalled at the thought. We were heavily interrupted last winter and our sites did what was required," said a major buyer.
Interruptible gas can be bought at a two to three pence a therm discount to firm gas, said Partridge.
"It was a good deal before (last winter), for several years people were never interrupted," he said.
Partridge expected the Network Code hard landing to push down the price of interruptible gas against firm gas.
"One would expect the differential to widen, it's increasingly attractive for the supplier to have a good portfolio of interruptible contracts to deal with daily balancing," he said.
